- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
There is a small, unspoken pact among strangers who walk through cities in winter: if you find a dropped glove on the sidewalk, you do not throw it away, and you do not leave it in the slush. You pick it up and perch it on the nearest fence post, drape it over a low branch, or set it delicately atop a fire hydrant. It sits there like a small wool flag, waving at waist height, waiting for a cold hand to retrace its steps.

I have always loved this quiet choreography of rescue. Nobody taught us to do it. There are no municipal signs instructing citizens on the proper elevation of lost knitwear. Yet across every cold climate, mittens bloom on iron railings after a snowstorm. It is a micro-monument to optimism—the belief that the person who lost this will come back, and that the world is just kind enough to hold it up for them until they do.

I started noticing other stray artifacts a few years ago, mostly by accident. It began with grocery lists left in the child seats of shopping carts. Once you look for them, you realize they are everywhere, tucked into the metal grating like secret dispatches.

A grocery list is perhaps the most honest literature we produce. Nobody writes one for posterity. There is no vanity in it, no curated self-image—just the raw, unadorned architecture of a week.

I keep a shoebox of them under my desk. One is written in neat, trembling cursive on the back of a bank envelope: *prunes, soup (not tomato), stamps, 60w bulbs.* Another is scrawled in thick black marker across torn cardboard: *ICE. LIMES. MORE ICE. PAPER TOWELS.* You can hear the party through the cardboard. You can feel the frantic afternoon heat, the host realizing an hour before guests arrive that the freezer is empty.

My favorite is written on a yellow sticky note, folded until the corners went soft. In tiny, careful block letters, it reads: *oat milk, avocados (check softness), basil, candles?, breath mints.*

That question mark beside *candles* carries an entire novel. Was it a first dinner cooked at home? An anniversary? A quiet apology? Did they buy the candles in the end, or stand in aisle four, suddenly self-conscious, and set them back on the shelf? I will never know. That is the strange pull of the shoebox: it holds dozens of lives paused right at the hinge of an ordinary Tuesday.

Beside the box sits a glass jar of orphan keys. I gather them from gutters, park benches, the dusty corners of laundromats. Some are dull silver, modern and flat, the kind that open apartment doors or cheap padlocks. Others are tarnished brass with ornate bows, heavy as old coins, belonging to cedar chests or houses long since torn down to make room for pharmacies.

There is a particular melancholy to a key separated from its lock. A broken mug is still recognizably a mug. A photograph of a stranger still offers a face. But a lost key is stranded potential. Its teeth were cut to match one exact, hidden geography of brass pins somewhere in the world. Without its companion, it is merely an oddly notched scrap of metal—a question whose answer has vanished.

Late at night, when sleep won’t come, I sometimes pour the jar onto the kitchen table and sort them by size. They make a crisp, bright clatter, like the sound of someone coming home. Somewhere out there are thirty or forty locks—rusted shut on garden sheds, bolted onto storage units, set into the doors of sunlit rooms—and I am holding the forgotten halves of their secrets.

We spend a great deal of our lives worrying about what we will leave behind. We try to build things that look permanent: careers, reputations, tidy rooms, carefully edited archives of our happiest afternoons. We want to be remembered for our grand gestures, the speeches we rehearsed, the monuments we meant to erect.

Yet I suspect the truest museum of humanity is made entirely of the things we dropped without noticing. Archaeologists know this. They love a royal tomb, certainly, but what makes them lean in close is a midden heap—a trash pit from three thousand years ago. A broken clay bowl with a potter’s thumbprint still pressed into the rim. A child’s toy carved from bone. A clay tablet complaining, in furious cuneiform, about a shipment of substandard copper. In those accidental remnants, the centuries collapse. You realize people have always been annoyed by bad deliveries, always hurried, always cold in winter, always hesitating over whether to buy candles.

It is raining lightly tonight, the kind of fine gray mist that makes streetlights wear halos. Earlier, walking back from the corner store with oranges and bread, I saw a blue knitted glove lying face-down near a storm drain. One finger was already dark with rainwater.

I shifted the bag to my left arm, stooped, and picked it up. It was small and smelled faintly of cedar and wet asphalt. Across the sidewalk ran a low brick wall topped with wrought iron. I shook the water from the wool and slid the glove gently onto a blunt iron finial, adjusting the thumb so it looked almost jaunty.

I stood for a moment, watching it against the wet dark. Probably no one will come back for it. By Thursday it will be stiff with frost; by next week it will vanish into the slow churn of the city.

Still, I walked home feeling lighter. Somewhere down the block, a hand was tucked deep inside a coat pocket, already missing its match. And behind me, on a wet iron fence, a small blue flag was waiting.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical first-person meditation turns ordinary lost objects into vivid signs of care, memory, and human connection.

## Grounded reading
The voice is tender, observant, and gently melancholy, with a recurring impulse to imagine the lives behind overlooked things. The prose lingers on tactile details—the rain-dark glove, the soft-folded shopping list, the bright clatter of keys—then gives them emotional weight without losing its lightness. It invites the reader to notice the small acts of care and the traces of anonymous lives that usually pass unnoticed.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds dropped gloves, abandoned grocery lists, orphaned keys, and archaeological debris as accidental records of ordinary life. Its moral emphasis is modest but clear: care can be enacted without recognition, and the everyday remnants people leave behind may preserve more human truth than deliberate monuments. The ending returns to the opening image, choosing quiet hope even while admitting the glove may never be reclaimed.

## Evidence line
> It is a micro-monument to optimism—the belief that the person who lost this will come back, and that the world is just kind enough to hold it up for them until they do.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sustained first-person collecting, tactile detail, and recurring transformation of lost objects into imagined lives make this sample’s choices notably coherent and distinctive.
